text.p: A parliamentary committee completed its draft of a post-communist constitution for Poland on Thursday. Three years in the making, the new charter will be submitted to the legislature and a national referendum.
Major parties hope to have it in force before elections late this year. But it may face opposition from rightwing Catholics who dislike its secular tone and want a constitutional ban on abortion.
Parliament's cross-party committee voted by 45 to two, with one abstention, to accept a version incorporating several major compromises hurried through in recent days.
Since the fall of communism in 1989, Poland has used an interim "small" constitution which supplemented or altered parts of the discredited communist-era document of 1952.
Attempts at a complete re-write were stalled by changes of government and fierce rows over its shape.

The ruling coalition of ex-communists and Peasants and the two largest opposition groups on the committee this week skirted or struck deals on problem issues so their version can have a chance of being adopted before the elections.
If the race is lost, a new parliament might start work from scratch, delaying the outcome still further.

Rightist Catholic parties, which were so split that they failed to enter parliament in 1993 elections and therefore had little say on the draft, want a charter founded on a religious idea of "natural law".

These parties, notably a strong new alliance around the Solidarity trade union, might well oppose the draft during the referendum unless major new changes are incorporated as it passes before an Assembly grouping both houses of parliament.
The two right-wingers who voted against the draft saw it as the fruit of compromise between centre-left opposition groups and the ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD).
"This is a fruit that is both unripe and rotten," PAP news agency quoted Solidarity's senator Piotr Andrzejewski as commenting.

Solidarity, which opposed last year's law easing abortion, wants protection of the unborn child in the constitution and wants the preamble to invoke God -- unlike the committee draft which recognises that some Poles are believers and other not.

At the last moment, the committee adopted some ideas from Solidarity's version, including a ban on communist or fascist totalitarian parties and a pledge that the state will stress the interests of the family.

Among new provisions, the current draft weakens the presidency, now held by ex-communist Aleksander Kwasniewski, by allowing his veto to be overruled by three fifths of lower house deputies rather than the current two-thirds, and reduces his influence on the armed forces.

It says that after two years, rulings by the Constitutional Tribunal, which assesses the compatibility of laws with the constitution, will be final and cannot be overturned by a parliamentary vote as they may be now.
It includes guarantees of free basic health care for all, regardless of income, and free education, although the draft admits the possibility of charges in higher state education.

Debate on the constitution is likely to be swept up into this year's election campaign, which will be largely fought on such issues as abortion. An 11-day visit by Pope John Paul ll to Poland from May 31 may also influence its course.
